body.text: Vietnam wants to become a strong maritime nation. Its new strategy makes clear that getting there will require more than ports and ships. It will also require institutions capable of deciding who can use an increasingly crowded sea, where, and on what terms.

Resolution 20, adopted in July 2026, marks an important shift in how Vietnam thinks about the sea. It calls for a move from exploiting marine resources towards modern marine governance, and from sector-by-sector management towards integrated governance of national marine space. Institutional reform is identified as a strategic breakthrough, together with science, technology, and high-quality human resources.

The economic stakes are considerable. With over 3,200 kilometres of coastline, Vietnam’s economic geography is already heavily maritime. Resolution 20 sets an ambitious target: for coastal provinces and cities to account for more than 70% of national GDP by 2030.

The strategy also aims for 6–10 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2030. But every turbine raises questions about access to marine space, interactions with fishing and shipping, transmission infrastructure, environmental impacts, and coastal communities. These competing claims are not hypothetical: Vietnam exported a record US$11.3 billion of seafood in 2025, while preparing for a potentially large offshore wind industry.
Investment alone cannot resolve these trade-offs.

The resolution acknowledges institutional challenges. Marine governance has not kept pace with development. Responsibilities overlap, inter-sectoral and inter-regional coordination remains weak, and marine science and human resources do not yet meet development needs.
Australia is already being urged to invest in the region’s capacity to govern emerging ocean industries.

Consider offshore wind. Building the industry requires coordination across marine spatial planning, electricity networks, ports, environmental assessment, fisheries, local industry, and investment regulation. Similar tensions arise as aquaculture, tourism, shipping, and conservation make competing claims on the same marine space.
Resolution 20 therefore calls for marine spatial planning to become a binding tool for coordinating uses of the sea, backed by stronger inter-agency coordination.

Implementation followed quickly. Just ten days after Resolution 20 was adopted, Vietnam’s government issued an action plan requiring revision of the Law on Marine and Island Resources and Environment, with an amended law to be submitted to the National Assembly in 2026. The proposed changes address important questions: how marine space is allocated and leased, what users will pay, and how competing claims are resolved.
This is the institutional infrastructure of a blue economy.

It also depends on people. Vietnam needs not only engineers, marine scientists, and environmental specialists, but also economists who understand ecological limits, planners capable of weighing competing uses of marine space, and managers who can negotiate among investors, regulators, and communities.
Here Australia has something useful to offer.

During the visit of Vietnam’s General Secretary and President Tô Lâm to Australia in August, the two countries agreed to enhance their Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. The joint statement commits the countries to deeper cooperation in marine science and monitoring and sustainable marine-resource management. It also calls for stronger cooperation in higher education, joint research, and professional development.
Rather than treating maritime cooperation, education, science, and climate as separate streams, Australia and Vietnam could bring them together around real marine-governance problems.

Joint interdisciplinary university programs could combine marine science with economics, environmental management, energy, and public policy. Executive education could bring together officials responsible for marine planning, fisheries, energy, environment, and investment. Joint policy laboratories could connect governments, universities, businesses, and coastal communities around actual marine-development decisions.
Australia is already being urged to invest in the region’s capacity to govern emerging ocean industries. Vietnam offers an opportunity to apply that principle on a larger scale.

This also reflects a changing bilateral relationship. Vietnam is a fast-growing middle-income economy seeking high-income status by 2045. Cooperation needs to extend beyond traditional development assistance towards building knowledge and institutions together.

Vietnam has the coastline, resources, and economic ambition to build a substantial blue economy. Whether it succeeds will depend on its ability to manage competing interests, protect marine natural capital, and turn new opportunities into broadly shared prosperity.

The infrastructure of Vietnam’s blue economy is therefore not only ports, vessels, and turbines. It is also institutions, knowledge, and people. Building that infrastructure could become a practical outcome of the Australia–Vietnam Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
